680.title: Passover: it would have been enough
680.hook: a song counting gifts one by one
680.tomorrow: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
680.howItsDone: At the seder, after the telling of the plagues, families sing Dayenu together, with everyone joining the chorus; in some Persian and Afghan Jewish homes, people playfully tap each other with scallions during the song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four children, and the one who doesn't know how to ask. Your line was answer each child. Did you answer someone where they were? Today, the loudest song of the night. Day six hundred eighty.

Partway through the seder, after a long stretch of reading, the energy in the room changes. Someone starts a song with a chorus of three syllables, and suddenly everyone, including the uncle who's been checking his phone and the toddler who's been under the table, is shouting it. Day, day, enu. Day, day, enu. In some Persian and Afghan Jewish families, people grab scallions from the table and playfully swat each other during the chorus, recalling the whips of slavery. It's the rowdiest moment of the night. And underneath the noise, the song is doing something careful: counting.
screen: `THE ENERGY CHANGES.` → `SCALLIONS IN THE AIR.` → `UNDERNEATH: COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Dayenu means it would have been enough for us. The song walks through the story of the Exodus in fifteen steps, each one a gift. If God had brought us out of Egypt, and not brought judgment on the Egyptians: dayenu. If God had split the sea for us, and not led us through it on dry ground: dayenu. If God had fed us manna, and not given us Shabbat. If God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah. All the way to the land of Israel and the Temple. Fifteen times, the table shouts: that would have been enough. The Haggadah introduces it with a line: how many good steps God has done for us. The oldest full version we have is in a prayer book from the ninth century, compiled by a scholar in Babylonia named Amram Gaon. Some of the lines sound strange if you take them literally. Would it really have been enough to stand at Sinai without the Torah? Teachers have answered in different ways. One answer is that the song isn't making a claim about history. It's training the eye. Any one of these steps, it says, deserved a whole thank-you of its own. Don't let the gifts blur into one big lump. And after the fifteen, the Haggadah adds a final paragraph that turns it around: how much more, then, should we be grateful, since God did all of them. Most of us give thanks in bulk, if at all. Dayenu gives thanks one gift at a time.
screen: `FIFTEEN STEPS, FIFTEEN GIFTS.` · `IF ONLY THIS, IT WOULD BE ENOUGH.` · `A NINTH-CENTURY PRAYER BOOK.` · `HOW MUCH MORE, FOR ALL OF THEM.` · then, large: `IT WOULD HAVE BEEN ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list gifts that would have been enough. Breathe. Think of one good thing in your life right now, maybe a person. Now break it into steps. If they had only shown up once: enough. If they had only stayed: enough. If they had only made you laugh that one time: enough. Go slowly, one gift at a time, saying dayenu after each, out loud or in your head. See how many steps you find before the bell. The bell holds the time.
Dayenu. It would have been enough for us: the seder's song of fifteen gifts, counted one by one. Today's word.
Your line: it would have been enough. Today, write down three small gifts from your day, each with its own dayenu. Day six hundred eighty.

681.title: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
681.hook: in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt
681.howItsDone: At the seder, the Haggadah reads the Mishnah's line that in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt; people recline and drink four cups as free people, and then sing the Psalms of Hallel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayenu, fifteen gifts counted one by one. Your line was it would have been enough. Did you write down three? Today, the line that makes the whole seder personal. Day six hundred eighty-one.

Most anniversaries look back. A wedding anniversary remembers a day that happened to two people. A national holiday remembers founders who are long gone. You honor them, but you weren't there. The seder could easily work the same way: here's what happened to our ancestors, three thousand years ago, pass the matzah. But there's a sentence in the Mishnah, said aloud at every seder, that refuses to let the story stay in the past tense. It doesn't ask you to remember the Exodus. It asks for something much stranger.
screen: `ANNIVERSARIES LOOK BACK.` → `YOU WEREN'T THERE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT REFUSES.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, at the end of the tractate on Passover, first gives Rabban Gamliel's rule: anyone who hasn't explained three things at the seder, the Passover offering, matzah and bitter herbs, hasn't fulfilled the duty of the night. Then it says: in every generation, a person is obligated to see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt. Not our ancestors. Me. And it proves it with the verse we met two days ago, in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me. When I came out. The verse speaks in the first person to people who were never slaves. Maimonides, in his version of this law, uses a slightly different word: a person must show himself as if he left. Show, not just see. That's why, he says, people recline at the seder, like free people at a banquet, and drink the cups. The body acts it out. And the Mishnah draws a conclusion. Because we came out, it says, we're obligated to thank and praise God. Then the seder breaks into the Psalms of praise. So remembering turns into gratitude, and gratitude into song. There's one more layer, from later Hasidic teachers. The Hebrew name for Egypt, Mitzrayim, sounds like meitzarim: narrow places, tight straits. So every person, they taught, has an Egypt: a narrow place they've been held. The seder asks each one to stand in the doorway of their own leaving, every year.
screen: `RABBAN GAMLIEL'S THREE THINGS.` · `IN EVERY GENERATION, AS IF YOU.` · `SEE IT, AND SHOW IT.` · `MITZRAYIM: THE NARROW PLACE.` · then, large: `AS IF YOU LEFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine leaving a narrow place. Sit back, the way someone free would sit. Breathe. Think of a narrow place you've been in: a job, an illness, a fear, a relationship, a season of your life when the walls felt close. Now picture the moment you stepped out, or the step you hope to take. Feel your shoulders open. You don't have to be fully out. Just stand in the doorway for a moment, as if you left. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, told in the first person, as if you yourself left. Today's word.
Your line: as if you left. Today, tell one part of your story in the present tense, as if it's still yours to walk through. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: Passover: Elijah's cup
682.hook: a cup is poured for Elijah and the door is opened
682.howItsDone: Near the end of the seder, after grace after meals, families fill a cup for Elijah and open the front door while reciting 'Pour out Your wrath' from the Psalms; some families now also place a cup of water for Miriam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's line, in every generation. Your line was as if you left. Did you tell part of your story in the present tense? Tonight, someone else is expected at the table. Day six hundred eighty-two.

It's late. The meal is over, the grace after meals is said, and the children are fading. Then someone fills a large, often beautiful cup that's been sitting untouched all night. A child is sent to open the front door. Cold air comes in. Everyone stands, or goes quiet, or sings. And the youngest kids watch the cup very closely, absolutely certain that if they look hard enough, they'll see the wine go down a little. Nobody at the table has invited this guest. He's been expected for about two and a half thousand years.
screen: `A CUP UNTOUCHED ALL NIGHT.` → `A CHILD OPENS THE DOOR.` → `WATCHING THE WINE.`

segments.voice: The guest is Elijah, the prophet. In the book of Kings, he doesn't die; he's carried up to heaven in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire. So in Jewish tradition, he never quite left. He turns up in Talmudic stories, disguised as a traveler, a beggar, a merchant. And the last prophet in the Hebrew Bible, Malachi, ends his book with a promise: God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD. In the old Jewish translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." So Elijah became the messenger of redemption. Why a cup? One explanation goes back to an old question: are there four cups at the seder, or five? Some versions of the Talmud mention a fifth. A popular later explanation says that since the question was never settled, a fifth cup is poured and not drunk, and it's named for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open. Why open the door? It's opened right before a passage asking God to pour out wrath on the nations that devoured Israel, words from the Psalms, said in years of real persecution. The Torah also calls this night a night of watching, so many say there's nothing to fear in opening the door. And Elijah, if he's coming, should find it open. In recent decades, some families have added a cup of water for Miriam, the prophet, beside Elijah's. Other families keep the older custom alone. Either way, the seder doesn't end with the door shut. It ends with it open, waiting.
screen: `ELIJAH NEVER DIED.` · `TURN THE HEARTS, MALACHI SAYS.` · `A FIFTH CUP, NOT DRUNK.` · `A NIGHT OF WATCHING.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE DOOR OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door for a minute. If you can, get up now and open a door or a window. Feel the air change. Stand there and breathe. Think of what you're waiting for: a reconciliation, a recovery, a turn in the world, a guest you haven't met yet. Malachi's promise was about hearts turning toward each other, parents to children, children to parents. Is there one heart you'd like turned toward you, or yours toward them? Leave the door open while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a night that ends with Elijah's cup poured and the door left open. Today's word.
Your line: leave the door open. Today, leave one small opening for someone: a message, an invitation, a seat. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: Passover: the Song of Songs
683.hook: a love poem read at Passover, which the rabbis read as God and Israel
683.tomorrow: The Omer: one quality a day
683.howItsDone: Many Ashkenazi synagogues read the Song of Songs aloud on the Shabbat during Passover, and many Sephardi and Mizrahi communities also chant it every Friday evening before Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elijah's cup and the open door. Your line was leave the door open. Did you leave an opening for someone? Today, the book read during the week of Passover. Day six hundred eighty-three.

Imagine opening a holy book and finding a love poem. Not a gentle one, either. Two lovers looking for each other through city streets at night. Descriptions of eyes like doves, hair like a flock of goats coming down a mountain. Kisses, perfume, a garden locked and then opened. A watchman in the streets. Nowhere in the eight chapters does God's name clearly appear. And yet this book sits in the Hebrew Bible, and every year, during the week of Passover, many synagogues read it out loud from beginning to end.
screen: `A LOVE POEM IN A HOLY BOOK.` → `EYES LIKE DOVES.` → `READ ALOUD AT PASSOVER.`

segments.voice: It's called Shir HaShirim, the Song of Songs: in Hebrew, that means the greatest song, the way holy of holies means the holiest place. In the second century, the rabbis debated which books belonged in the Bible, and some had doubts about this one. Rabbi Akiva answered with a famous line, in the Mishnah: all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. He and the rabbis after him read it as a love song between God and the people Israel. The ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, goes further and reads the poem as Israel's history, beginning with the Exodus. So why at Passover? The plainest reason is the season. In the old Jewish translation, the beloved calls: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of singing is come." Passover is the spring festival, and this is a spring poem. The deeper reason is the story. In the rabbis' reading, the Exodus is the beginning of the romance: God takes Israel out of Egypt and into the wilderness, like a bride following her beloved. So on the festival of leaving, the community reads a book about two who long for each other. One verse sums it up for many readers: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Among Ashkenazim, it's usually read on the Shabbat during the festival. Many Sephardi communities also chant it every Friday evening, as Shabbat comes in. Read as a love poem, it's beautiful. Read as a parable, it says that faith is not only obedience. It's longing, on both sides.
screen: `SHIR HASHIRIM: THE GREATEST SONG.` · `AKIVA: THE HOLY OF HOLIES.` · `THE WINTER IS PAST.` · `MY BELOVED IS MINE.` · then, large: `THE SONG OF SONGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of love. If you can, find one: a line from a poem, a letter you kept, a text someone sent you once, or one of today's verses. Read it slowly, twice. Then sit with whoever it makes you think of: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, or, if you pray, God. Notice the longing in it, and let it be good rather than sad. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The spring festival of leaving Egypt, when many read the Song of Songs, a love poem between God and Israel. Today's word.
Your line: the song of songs. Today, send one person a line of love, a poem, a song, or your own plain words. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: The Omer: one quality a day
684.hook: the mystics pair each of the forty-nine days with a quality to refine
684.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, observant Jews count the Omer each evening with a blessing, naming the day and week; many also follow the Kabbalistic chart of sefirot, reflecting on one quality each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs, read in the week of Passover. Your line was the song of songs. Did you send a line of love? Today, the seven weeks that run from Passover to Shavuot. Day six hundred eighty-four.

Every evening for seven weeks, after nightfall, observant Jews say a blessing and then a number. Today is one day of the Omer. Today is two days. Today is eight days, which is one week and one day. Miss a whole day, and by many rulings you keep counting but stop saying the blessing. It sounds like the world's most patient countdown. Apps and wall charts and little calendars on the fridge help people keep track. But a countdown usually means you're waiting for something. The mystics turned these forty-nine days into something closer to a training plan.
screen: `A BLESSING, THEN A NUMBER.` → `FORTY-NINE NIGHTS.` → `A COUNTDOWN, OR A TRAINING PLAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Torah. In Leviticus, from the day the first sheaf of barley is brought, the omer, you count. In the old Jewish translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete." Then, on the fiftieth day, comes Shavuot, the feast of weeks. In the rabbis' reading, it's the road from leaving Egypt to receiving the Torah at Sinai. Freedom first; then what to do with it. The word for counting is sefirah. And this is where the mystics come in. In the Kabbalah, a very similar word, sefirot, names the qualities through which God is revealed in the world. The lower seven are usually listed as: chesed, loving-kindness. Gevurah, strength or restraint. Tiferet, beauty and balance. Netzach, endurance. Hod, humility, or splendor. Yesod, foundation, the bond between people. And malchut, kingship: presence, the way it all shows up in the world. Seven qualities, seven weeks. And inside each week, seven days. So the first week is loving-kindness, and its first day is loving-kindness within loving-kindness. The second day, strength within loving-kindness: love that knows its limits. And so on, forty-nine combinations, one each night. Kabbalists and Hasidic teachers built a practice on it, and many teachers of character, middot, still use it today: each day, look at one quality in yourself and refine it a little. Not all of it. Just today's square on the chart. The counting stops being a wait. It becomes the preparation. By the time you reach the mountain, you've worked, quality by quality, on the person who's arriving.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS COMPLETE.` · `FROM EGYPT TO SINAI.` · `SEVEN QUALITIES, SEVEN DAYS.` · `ONE SQUARE ON THE CHART.` · then, large: `REFINE ONE QUALITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: work on one quality today. Breathe, and choose one: kindness, restraint, balance, endurance, humility, connection, or presence. Pick the one that's been weakest lately, or the one that's been too strong. Think of a single moment today when it'll be tested. A meeting, a dinner, a drive. Picture yourself meeting that moment with the quality a little more refined. Just a little. The bell holds the time.
Sefirah. Counting: the forty-nine days of the Omer, and for the mystics, one quality refined each day. Today's word.
Your line: refine one quality. Today, at the moment your chosen quality is tested, take one breath first. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: Lag BaOmer
685.hook: the thirty-third day breaks the mourning with bonfires, linked to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
685.howItsDone: On Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer, the season's mourning customs are lifted: weddings and haircuts resume, bonfires are lit, especially in Israel, and many make pilgrimage to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's tomb in Meron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sefirah, the counting of the Omer, one quality a day. Your line was refine one quality. Did you take a breath before the test? Today, the thirty-third night of the count. Day six hundred eighty-five.

For weeks, the season has been quiet. In many communities, there have been no weddings, no live music, no haircuts. People look a little shaggy. Then, on one night in late spring, all over Israel, the sky fills with smoke. Kids have been collecting scrap wood for days: broken pallets, old doors, fruit crates. Bonfires burn in parks and empty lots. Families roast potatoes in the coals. In the north, at the foot of a mountain, huge crowds pour into a small town to sing and dance around a tomb. And the next morning, the barbers are busy, and wedding halls are full.
screen: `WEEKS WITHOUT WEDDINGS OR MUSIC.` → `BONFIRES ALL OVER THE COUNTRY.` → `A CROWD AT A TOMB.`

segments.voice: Lag BaOmer means the thirty-third of the Omer. Hebrew letters are also numbers: lamed is thirty, gimel is three, and together they're said lag. On this day, the mourning customs of the Omer season, which we'll explore tomorrow, are lifted. Why the thirty-third day? The honest answer is that the reasons came after the custom. One tradition from the Middle Ages says it was the day a plague among Rabbi Akiva's students stopped. A later tradition, from the mystics of Safed in the 1500s, says it's the anniversary of the death of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, one of Akiva's students. The Talmud tells a famous story about him. He criticized the Roman rulers, was sentenced to death, and hid with his son in a cave for twelve years. A carob tree and a spring of water appeared to keep them alive. They studied all day, buried in sand up to their necks to save their clothes. Tradition credits Rabbi Shimon with the Zohar, the central book of the Kabbalah. Most historians date the Zohar to thirteenth-century Spain and link it to Moses de León. Many traditional Jews hold to the older attribution. The mystics taught that on the day he died, Rabbi Shimon revealed his deepest secrets, and the house was filled with light. So the day of a death became a celebration, a hilula, a wedding-feast of a soul. And the bonfires are said to recall his light. His tomb is in Meron, in the Galilee, which is why the crowds go there. Children in some communities get their first haircut there, and play with bows and arrows. After weeks of quiet, Lag BaOmer is a break in the sadness.
screen: `LAMED-GIMEL: THIRTY-THREE.` · `REASONS CAME AFTER THE CUSTOM.` · `TWELVE YEARS IN A CAVE.` · `A DEATH DAY TURNED TO LIGHT.` · then, large: `A BREAK IN THE SADNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit by a fire or candle. If you can, light a candle now, safely, or sit by a fireplace, or just watch a flame on a screen. Let your eyes rest on it. Breathe. Think of a long stretch that's been heavy for you, or for someone close to you. You don't have to end it. Just let this one minute be a break in it: warmth, light, nothing to fix. The bell holds the time.
Lag BaOmer. The thirty-third day of the Omer: bonfires, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and a break in the season's mourning. Today's word.
Your line: a break in the sadness. Today, give someone who's going through a hard stretch one small bright moment: a call, a treat, a joke. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: Why the Omer mourns (Yevamot 62b)
686.hook: the Talmud says Akiva's students died in these weeks for not honoring each other
686.howItsDone: During part of the Omer period, many Jews refrain from weddings, haircuts and live music in mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students; Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently, and many lift the customs on Lag BaOmer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lag BaOmer, bonfires and Rabbi Shimon. Your line was a break in the sadness. Did you give someone a bright moment? Today, the sadness itself: why these weeks mourn at all. Day six hundred eighty-six.

Picture the greatest school of its age. One teacher, Rabbi Akiva, the most famous scholar of his generation, and thousands upon thousands of students, spread across the land from the hills in the north to the coastal plain. Brilliant people. People who argued about every letter of the Torah and memorized whole tractates. If any group seemed set to carry the tradition forward, it was this one. And according to the Talmud, in a few weeks between Passover and Shavuot, almost all of them died. The Talmud's explanation isn't about war, or a lack of learning. It's about how they treated each other.
screen: `THE GREATEST SCHOOL OF ITS AGE.` → `THOUSANDS OF STUDENTS.` → `GONE IN A FEW WEEKS.`

segments.voice: The passage is in tractate Yevamot, page 62b. Rabbi Akiva, it says, had twelve thousand pairs of students. Students learned in pairs, so that's twenty-four thousand. And all of them died in one period, because they did not treat each other with respect. The Talmud adds: they died between Passover and Shavuot. And the world, it says, was desolate. Then Akiva went south and taught just five new students. Among them were Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whom we met yesterday. Those five carried the Torah forward. Now hear the irony. Rabbi Akiva is the one who called the verse from Leviticus, in the old Jewish translation, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," a great principle of the Torah. His own students, the Talmud says, failed at exactly that. They knew the texts. They didn't honor the people learning beside them. Some historians suggest the deaths may also reflect the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome, in which Akiva supported the rebels; the Talmud doesn't say so. Either way, the rabbis chose to remember it as a lesson about respect. That's why, in many communities, these weeks carry quiet mourning: no weddings, no haircuts, no live music, for part of the Omer. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently. And many teachers turn the mourning into a task. If the students died for lack of honoring each other, the repair is to honor each other more. Especially, they say, the people you argue with.
screen: `TWELVE THOUSAND PAIRS.` · `NO RESPECT FOR EACH OTHER.` · `FIVE STUDENTS IN THE SOUTH.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR, AKIVA TAUGHT.` · then, large: `HONOR EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone today. Breathe, and think of someone you work, study or live beside, especially someone you disagree with, or compete with, or take for granted. Picture their face. Now name one thing about them that deserves honor: their effort, their honesty, their patience, a skill you don't have. Hold that thought until it feels true. Then decide how you'll show it today, in words or in a small act. The bell holds the time.
Why the Omer mourns. For Akiva's students, who, the Talmud says, died for not honoring each other. Today's word.

Your line: honor each other. A week of enough, as if you left, an open door, a song of songs, one quality, a break in the sadness, and now honor. Today, tell the person you pictured the thing you honor in them. Day six hundred eighty-six.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Akiva. twenty-four thousand students are gone, and the world feels desolate. what do you do?
options: stop teaching.
go south and teach five new students.
write down everything you know and retire.
fork.reveal: he went south and taught five students, among them Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon, and through them the Torah went on.

original.note: Hebrew: because they did not treat one another with honor, the Talmud's reason.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Omer is a sad season for no clear reason.
what it means: it mourns Akiva's students, who died for not honoring each other.
what a scholar hears: Yevamot 62b's twelve thousand pairs, from Gevat to Antipatris; some historians connect the deaths to the Bar Kokhba revolt.
